models.family: serve-success lift with a Monte Carlo winning probability and an exponential leverage average
models.purpose: Turn each ball into a winning probability and a momentum for both players.
models.summary: Short-term motivation raises the next serve success rate in proportion to the consecutive points just won, and the paper keeps only orders of three and below because higher orders rarely appear. A confidence factor then blends the historical grass-court serve rate into the current rate through a tuning parameter, so the career record dominates early and fades. The two are combined by substituting the confidence rate for the unmotivated rate. Because a tennis point is uncertain, a Monte Carlo of 1000 runs climbs from the ball to the game, the set, and the match, and the winning rate after a ball is the wins divided by the runs. Leverage is the change in that rate from winning the point rather than losing it, and its sign names the player rather than the size. Momentum is the exponential moving average of the leverage a player has gained, so the newest point weighs most.

models.section: 6.1 The runs test and the contingency table
models.family: runs test for randomness with a chi-square contingency check
models.purpose: Test whether the scoring sequence is random and whether it moves with the momentum.
models.summary: Each point in a game is coded 1 when player A won it and 0 otherwise, and a run is a streak of the same code. The test asks whether the number of runs is what a random arrangement would give, with the expectation and the variance written out and the statistic referred to a standard normal. Applied to every game, 45.11 percent of games reject randomness at the 90 percent level. A second check crosses who won the point with whose momentum was larger, and the chi-square of 5.566 with a level of 0.018 rejects independence at the same confidence. No formula is printed for the chi-square itself.

models.family: grid-searched random forest for the direction of the next swing
models.purpose: Call whether the advantage shifts in the next stretch of points, and toward whom.
models.summary: A reversal point is the nearest zero of the momentum lying between a peak of one player and a peak of the other, found with the peak routine. The order of the peaks sets the label: 1 when the advantage turns toward the player, -1 when it turns toward the opponent, and 0 when the point is not a turn. Two groups of indicators, one player's own and the shared ones, with the second player mirroring the first, are fed to a random forest whose depth, leaf size, split size, and tree count are chosen by an exhaustive search. On an 8 to 2 split the search returns no depth limit, a leaf of 1, a split of 3, and 100 trees, and the accuracy reaches 94 percent, with only 3 points missed and no turn ever called as the opposite turn. The opponent's total score ranks as the most relevant indicator.

assumptions: The three labels cover every point.
The derived indicators are computable from the given ones.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The best parameter set and the accuracy are printed. The individual trees are not.

models.family: principal-component extraction with a varimax rotation
models.purpose: Reduce the many swing indicators to a few factors a coach can compare.
models.summary: The importances are too many for a coach to use, so the top 15 are tested for factorability. Bartlett's statistic is 11512.67 on 105 degrees of freedom with a probability of 0, which rejects the identity at the 95 percent level, and the sampling adequacy is 0.708, which the paper reads as adequate by Kaiser's standard. The scree plot flattens at four components, so four are kept and rotated by the varimax rule under Kaiser normalization. They are named from their heaviest loads: expenditure from points, rallies, and distance; technical from break and net conversion; running distance from the per-point distance; and game situation from the games won.

equation_status.reason: The adequacy and the sphericity are printed as values. No extraction equation is printed.

objectives: Hand the coach a few named factors instead of the full indicator list.
constraints: The count is chosen where the scree contribution becomes small.
Each factor is named from its heaviest loads.

parameter_estimation.method: The factor count is read off the scree plot. No loading is estimated by hand.

steps: Keep the fifteen most important indicators.
Run the adequacy and the sphericity tests.
Extract components and stop at four.
Rotate by varimax and name each factor from its loads.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Four factors; sampling adequacy 0.708; sphericity 11512.67 with probability 0.

assumptions: The top fifteen indicators are enough to represent the swing.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Both suitability tests are printed and passed, and the four factors are named from the rotated loads.
